archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose down-to-down efficiency is top-five in the league. Its 6-4 record trails that efficiency because of close losses, giveaways and some of the worst special teams in football, and this year the defense is carrying more of the load than McVay's offense.

report.headline: Elite run defense and a pristine line, undercut by giveaways and special teams
report.take:
These Rams are not last year's version. In 2025 the offense led the league in scoring and finished second in EPA, and the team ranked first in net EPA. This season the offense has slipped to 11th in EPA, and the identity has moved to the other side of the ball. The defense ranks 4th in EPA allowed and first in rush EPA allowed on a play-by-play basis, and it holds offenses to 31.6% on third down. Net EPA is still 5th, which is a contender's profile. The record just hasn't caught up: a +61 point differential implies seven wins, not six.

The gap between the efficiency and the 6-4 record comes from a few leaks. The offense has given the ball away 15 times against 12 takeaways. Special teams cost them 3.22 EPA a game, 30th in the league. They are 0.4 in one-score games. Three of the four losses came by four points or fewer, including the 18-16 home loss to Arizona as 12.5-point favorites, and Week 1's 27-7 loss to San Francisco is the only real beating on the schedule. That pattern points to noise more than a flaw. It is the reverse of 2023 and 2024, when this franchise won more games than its differential said it should.

The numbers hide two things. First, the defense is far better at preventing plays than at disrupting them. It ranks 27th in pressure rate and 31st in QB hit rate, and it wins with coverage and tackling: 3rd in EPA allowed on deep passes, 9th in missed-tackle rate. That works until a quarterback gets time and finds his third receiver, and WR3s score 5 PPR points a game over their average against this unit, last in the league. Second, the offensive line has been the league's best at keeping pressure off Stafford, at 13.9% (1st), and it has the lowest stuff rate. That line is now losing its starting center Coleman Shelton (doubtful, out several weeks), left guard Steve Avila (out) and the backup center Dylan McMahon (IR). The interior that made everything clean is being rebuilt on the fly.

The trend is good. Since the Arizona upset the Rams have won every game, and the defense has turned the corner on the pass rush with 4 and 5 sacks in the last two. The closing stretch is brutal, though: Kansas City, at San Francisco, two Seattle games and a trip to Tampa's 2nd-ranked defense. A team this efficient should make the playoffs. Whether it does it comfortably depends on the line holding up and on stopping the giveaways.

strengths.title: Run defense that erases offenses
strengths.body: The Rams rank first in play-by-play rush EPA allowed and 4th in explosive run rate allowed, and the lead back's touches against them are among the least productive in the league. It forces opponents into long passing downs, which feeds the 4th-ranked third-down defense. The Buffalo game, with 234 rushing yards allowed, is the one outlier, so this looks structural rather than schedule-driven.

strengths.title: League-best protection and run blocking
strengths.body: Stafford has been pressured on 13.9% of dropbacks, the lowest rate in the league. The stuff rate is also first and yards per carry is 4th. That keeps the offense 4th in success rate even though its EPA is only mid-pack. It is the strength most at risk right now, with two interior starters and the backup center hurt.

strengths.title: Coverage that takes away the deep ball
strengths.body: Even without a pass rush, the back end allows almost nothing downfield: 3rd in deep-pass EPA allowed and 4th in overall pass EPA. Opposing WR1s and tight ends score below their averages. This is disciplined zone play rather than a rush-driven mirage, so it should travel.

concerns.title: Interior line suddenly gutted
concerns.body: Shelton (92% of snaps) is set to miss several weeks, and Avila (91%) is out. McMahon, the next center up, is on IR with a partially torn patella. The league's cleanest pocket and best run blocking were built on that interior, so expect more pressure and more stuffed runs until the starters return. This is the single biggest threat to the offense.

concerns.title: Giveaways and special teams bleed
concerns.body: Fifteen turnovers leave the Rams -3 in turnover margin. Special teams rank 30th in EPA, and the long snapper is also hurt. Neither is a defining trait of good teams, and turnover luck tends to even out, but both have directly swung close losses. They matter more against a ball-hawking opponent.

concerns.title: No consistent pass rush
concerns.body: The defense ranks 27th in pressure rate and 31st in QB hit rate. Quarterbacks with time can work the middle of the field, and the WR3 hole is the league's worst. The recent sack games are encouraging but small samples, so this is a real flaw the coverage has been masking.

trend.note: After a 2-4 start that included the home upset by Arizona, the Rams have won every game since, capped by a 34-6 rout in Arizona with five sacks and 202 rushing yards. Most of those wins came against middling or bad opponents, and the schedule now stiffens sharply.

nextGame.headline: Rams' run wall meets a Packers offense that can't run
nextGame.body:
Two 6-4 teams with opposite profiles meet indoors in Los Angeles, the Rams coming off the bye with ten days of rest. Green Bay's run game is the worst in the league by EPA, 31st in yards per carry and 28th in stuff rate. Against the league's top run defense, that should leave Jordan Love throwing on obvious downs. Love can do that: the Packers rank 9th in pass EPA and get the ball out fast. The Packers' record leans on things that tend to fade. They are 0.75 in one-score games, sit +0.9 a game in turnover margin and have 1.32 wins over expected. Their defense is a bend-and-take-it-away unit, 2nd in takeaways and 3rd in sacks, but 26th in red-zone touchdown rate and 21st on third down.

Availability cuts both ways. The Rams' interior is depleted with Shelton doubtful, Avila out and McMahon on IR, right as they face a defense that has 26 sacks. Davante Adams is targeting this game for his return from IR, which would give Stafford a second real target next to Puka Nacua. Green Bay is without linebacker Zaire Franklin (99% of snaps), guard Sean Rhyan and Josh Jacobs. Micah Parsons is listed out but said to be near a debut, and if he plays he is aimed squarely at the Rams' weakest spot. The Book has no line posted yet.

waysToWin.title: Make Green Bay one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: The Packers already can't run, and the Rams own the league's best run defense. Without Jacobs, Green Bay should be throwing on long downs into a coverage unit that allows almost nothing deep. Win early downs and the 4th-ranked third-down defense takes over.

waysToWin.title: Feed Nacua against a soft WR1 matchup
waysToWin.body: Green Bay's defense ranks 26th against opposing WR1s by PPR over average, and Nacua has dominated the target share when healthy. The Packers' pass defense limits explosives, so a steady short-to-intermediate diet to Nacua, plus Adams if he's back, fits both the matchup and a line that needs the ball out quickly. Tight end is the place not to force it, since Green Bay is first against TE1s.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: The Packers give up touchdowns on 69% of red-zone trips, 26th in the league, and lose Franklin from the middle of that defense. The Rams' backs, Williams and Corum, can punish a linebacker group missing its every-down player once the offense gets close.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers hand Green Bay short fields
waysToLose.body: The Packers are 2nd in takeaways and 3rd in turnover margin, and the Rams have given it away 15 times. In a game between closely matched efficiency profiles, a two-giveaway day is the most likely way the Rams lose.

waysToLose.title: Patched interior can't hold the rush
waysToLose.body: With the starting center and left guard out, Green Bay's 3rd-ranked sack total becomes a real problem, more so if Parsons debuts. Interior pressure breaks the timing Stafford relies on and forces the obvious passing downs this offense has mostly avoided.

waysToLose.title: Love picks apart a quiet rush
waysToLose.body: The Rams rarely hit the quarterback, and Love gets the ball out among the fastest in the league. With time, he can attack the slot and third receivers, where the Rams rank last. Add the Rams' special-teams leaks and a quiet defensive day turns a close game the wrong way.

nextGame.watch: Who snaps the ball and plays left guard for the Rams, and whether Green Bay's pass rush, with or without Parsons, can live in the A-gaps.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real. A top-five net EPA team with an elite run defense, sturdy coverage and a strong (if temporarily damaged) line should keep winning more than it loses, and the close-loss and turnover luck should even out somewhat. The problem is the schedule. Kansas City, a trip to San Francisco's top offense, two games against Seattle's 5th-ranked defense and a trip to Tampa's 2nd-ranked defense leave few easy afternoons, with only Dallas's last-ranked defense standing out as a soft spot.

The division is probably out of reach with San Francisco at 8-1, so the realistic target is a wild card, and the Seattle home-and-home could decide it. Expect scoring to dip a bit while the interior line is patched and the schedule hardens. Points allowed should stay near where they are, because a defense built on run stopping and deep coverage holds up better than one built on turnovers. Special teams is unlikely to fix itself midseason.
swingFactors: Return timeline for Shelton and Avila
Two Seattle games for wild-card position

confidence.note: Ten games of strong efficiency data, but key interior-line injuries and a much harder closing schedule add real uncertainty.
